q: The area between a velocity–time graph and the time axis gives the body's:
x: Area = velocity × time, which has the unit of length, so it gives the displacement. The slope of the same graph gives the acceleration, the usual mix-up.

q: A body moves along a straight line with uniform velocity. Its velocity–time graph is:
o: A straight line sloping upward through the origin
x: Uniform velocity means v does not change with time, so the graph is parallel to the time axis (zero slope, zero acceleration). A rising straight line describes uniform acceleration.

q: A car travels 30 km due east in 0.5 h and then 10 km due west in the next 0.5 h. Its average velocity for the whole trip is:
x: Net displacement = 30 − 10 = 20 km due east in a total of 1 h, so average velocity = 20 km h⁻¹ due east. Using the total distance 40 km gives the average speed, 40 km h⁻¹, not the velocity.

q: The velocity–time graph of a car is a straight line rising from 10 m s⁻¹ at t = 0 to 30 m s⁻¹ at t = 5 s. The distance covered in these 5 s is:
x: Area of the trapezium = ½(10 + 30) × 5 = 100 m; check with s = ut + ½at², a = 4 m s⁻²: 50 + 50 = 100 m. Forgetting the ½ gives 200 m; using only the final speed gives 150 m.

q: The velocity–time graph of a body moving along a straight line is a straight line from +10 m s⁻¹ at t = 0 to −10 m s⁻¹ at t = 4 s. In these 4 s, the distance travelled and the magnitude of the displacement are:
x: The velocity is zero at t = 2 s. Area from 0 to 2 s = ½ × 10 × 2 = +10 m; from 2 to 4 s = −10 m. Distance = 10 + 10 = 20 m; displacement = 10 − 10 = 0. Adding the areas with their signs for the distance gives zero by mistake.

q: The displacement–time graph of a body is a straight line through the origin with a slope of 3 m s⁻¹. The body has:
o: A uniform acceleration of 3 m s⁻²
A velocity that increases by 3 m s⁻¹ every second
A uniform velocity of 3 m s⁻¹ and zero acceleration
x: The slope of a displacement–time graph is the velocity; a constant slope means a constant velocity of 3 m s⁻¹ and so zero acceleration. Reading the slope as an acceleration gives the 3 m s⁻² option.

q: A ball is thrown vertically upward. Ignoring air resistance, at the highest point of its flight the ball has:
o: Zero velocity and an acceleration g downward
Zero velocity and an acceleration g upward
x: At the top the ball is momentarily at rest, but gravity still acts, so its acceleration is g vertically downward throughout. Believing zero velocity means zero acceleration is the classic error.

q: A car moves at 20 m s⁻¹ for 10 s, stands still for 10 s, then moves at 10 m s⁻¹ for 20 s in the same direction. Its average speed for the whole 40 s is:
x: Distance = 20 × 10 + 0 + 10 × 20 = 400 m in 40 s, so average speed = 10 m s⁻¹. Averaging the two speeds gives 15 m s⁻¹; leaving out the 10 s stop gives 400/30 = 40/3 m s⁻¹.

q: A body starts from rest and accelerates uniformly to 10 m s⁻¹ in 2 s, moves at 10 m s⁻¹ for 4 s, then slows uniformly to rest in 4 s. Its average velocity over the 10 s is:
x: Displacement = area under the v–t graph = ½(10)(2) + 10 × 4 + ½(10)(4) = 10 + 40 + 20 = 70 m; check as a trapezium: ½(4 + 10) × 10 = 70 m. Average velocity = 70/10 = 7 m s⁻¹. Averaging 0 and 10 m s⁻¹ gives 5 m s⁻¹.

q: Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², the distance a body falls from rest in the first 2 s is:
x: s = ½gt² = ½ × 10 × 2² = 20 m. Forgetting the ½ gives 40 m; forgetting to square t gives 10 m.

q: A car speeds up uniformly from 10 m s⁻¹ to 30 m s⁻¹ while covering 100 m. Its acceleration is:
x: v² = u² + 2as: 900 = 100 + 200a, so a = 4 m s⁻². Check: t = (30 − 10)/4 = 5 s and average speed 20 m s⁻¹ × 5 s = 100 m. Using (v − u)² = 400 instead of v² − u² gives 2 m s⁻².

q: A stone dropped from rest from a height h takes time t to reach the ground. Ignoring air resistance, a stone dropped from a height 4h takes:
x: h = ½gt², so t ∝ √h; four times the height gives √4 = 2 times the time. Taking t ∝ h gives 4t.

q: A car braking with a constant deceleration stops in a time t from a speed v. With the same deceleration, the time it takes to stop from a speed 2v is:
x: From v = u + at with final speed zero, t = u/a, so the stopping time is proportional to the initial speed: 2t. The stopping distance (∝ u²) would become four times, which gives the tempting 4t.

q: A stone is thrown vertically upward at 20 m s⁻¹ from the top of a tower 25 m high. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², it reaches the ground at the foot of the tower after:
x: Taking up as positive: −25 = 20t − 5t², so t² − 4t − 5 = 0 and t = 5 s. Check: it rises for 2 s to 20 m above the top (45 m above ground), then falls 45 m in 3 s; total 5 s. 4 s is only the time to come back to the top of the tower.

q: A ball is thrown vertically upward and reaches a greatest height of 45 m. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², its speed when it is at half this height on the way up is:
x: Launch speed: u² = 2gH = 900, so u = 30 m s⁻¹. At 22.5 m: v² = 900 − 2 × 10 × 22.5 = 450, so v = 15√2 m s⁻¹. Check by energy: half the kinetic energy is left, so v = u/√2. Halving the speed gives the tempting 15 m s⁻¹.

q: A train slows uniformly from 30 m s⁻¹ to 10 m s⁻¹ over a distance of 200 m. The time this takes is:
x: Average velocity = (30 + 10)/2 = 20 m s⁻¹, so t = 200/20 = 10 s. Check: a = (10² − 30²)/(2 × 200) = −2 m s⁻² and t = (10 − 30)/(−2) = 10 s. Dividing 200 m by the final speed gives 20 s.

q: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 30 m s⁻¹. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², its height above the point of projection 4 s later is:
x: s = ut − ½gt² = 30 × 4 − 5 × 16 = 120 − 80 = 40 m. Check: it reaches 45 m at 3 s and falls 5 m in the next second. 50 m is the total distance travelled (45 + 5), not the height.

q: A body falls freely in a vacuum near the Earth's surface. Which quantity stays constant during its fall?
x: In free fall the only force is the weight, so the acceleration is constant at g. Velocity, momentum and kinetic energy all increase as it falls.

q: According to Newton's third law, the action and reaction forces between two bodies:
o: Act on the same body and cancel each other
Act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other
Are equal only when the bodies are at rest
x: Action and reaction are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and act on different bodies, so they cannot cancel. Thinking they act on the same body and cancel is the common misconception.

q: A car of mass 1000 kg accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m s⁻¹ in 10 s. The net force on it is:
x: a = (20 − 0)/10 = 2 m s⁻², so F = ma = 1000 × 2 = 2000 N; check: F = Δp/Δt = 20 000/10 = 2000 N. Multiplying mass by the final speed gives 20 000 N (the momentum, not the force).

q: The force on a ball during a kick rises uniformly from zero to 100 N in 0.2 s and then stops. The impulse given to the ball is:
x: Impulse = area under the force–time graph = ½ × 100 × 0.2 = 10 N s. Using the peak force for the whole time gives 20 N s.

q: A cricketer catching a fast ball pulls his hands backward as he catches it. This reduces the force on his hands because it:
o: Reduces the change in the ball's momentum
Increases the time over which the ball's momentum is reduced to zero
Increases the impulse on the ball
x: The change in momentum (the impulse) is fixed by the ball's mass and speed; spreading it over a longer time makes F = Δp/Δt smaller. The momentum change itself is not reduced.

q: A 3 kg block on a smooth horizontal table is tied by a light string, passing over a smooth pulley at the table's edge, to a 2 kg mass hanging freely. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the tension in the string is:
x: Only the hanging weight drives both: a = 20/(3 + 2) = 4 m s⁻²; the string accelerates the 3 kg block, so T = 3 × 4 = 12 N. Check on the hanging mass: 20 − T = 2 × 4, so T = 12 N. Taking T equal to the weight, 20 N, ignores the acceleration.

q: A horizontal jet of water strikes a wall at 10 m s⁻¹ and stops without bouncing back. 2 kg of water hits the wall every second. The force of the water on the wall is:
x: F = rate of change of momentum = (mass per second) × change in velocity = 2 × 10 = 20 N. 40 N would need the water to rebound at 10 m s⁻¹.

q: A force F gives a 2 kg mass an acceleration of 6 m s⁻², and gives a second mass an acceleration of 2 m s⁻². If the two masses are tied together, the same force gives them an acceleration of:
x: F = 2 × 6 = 12 N, so the second mass is 12/2 = 6 kg. Together: a = 12/(2 + 6) = 1.5 m s⁻². Subtracting or adding the two accelerations (4 or 8 m s⁻²) is the slip.

q: A 0.5 kg ball dropped from a height of 5 m rebounds to a height of 1.25 m. It is in contact with the floor for 0.1 s. Ignoring air resistance and the ball's weight during the contact, and taking g = 10 m s⁻², the average force of the floor on the ball is:
x: Speed before impact = √(2 × 10 × 5) = 10 m s⁻¹ downward; after = √(2 × 10 × 1.25) = 5 m s⁻¹ upward. Δp = 0.5 × (10 + 5) = 7.5 N s, so F = 7.5/0.1 = 75 N. Subtracting the speeds, as if both were in the same direction, gives 25 N.

q: Which of these collisions is very nearly elastic?
o: A bullet embedding itself in a wooden block
A collision between two molecules of an ideal gas
A lump of wet clay hitting the floor
x: In an elastic collision kinetic energy is conserved; collisions of ideal-gas molecules are treated as perfectly elastic. In the others the bodies stick or deform, so kinetic energy is lost and the collisions are inelastic.

q: A very heavy body moving at speed v makes a head-on elastic collision with a very light body at rest. Just after the collision, the light body moves with a speed of about:
x: For a head-on elastic collision, v₂ = 2m₁u₁/(m₁ + m₂); with m₁ ≫ m₂ this is about 2u₁ = 2v. Check: the heavy body keeps about v, and the relative speed of separation must equal the approach speed v, so the light body moves at v + v = 2v.

q: A body moving with kinetic energy K collides with an identical body at rest, and the two stick together. The kinetic energy lost in the collision is:
x: Momentum: mu = 2mV, so V = u/2. Kinetic energy after = ½(2m)(u/2)² = ¼mu² = K/2, so K/2 is lost. Zero would be true only for an elastic collision.

q: A 10 g bullet moving horizontally at 300 m s⁻¹ embeds itself in a 0.99 kg wooden block hanging at rest from long strings. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the block with the bullet swings up to a height of:
x: Momentum: 0.01 × 300 = (0.01 + 0.99)V, so V = 3 m s⁻¹. Then ½V² = gh gives h = 9/20 = 0.45 m. Kinetic energy is not conserved in the impact, only during the swing. Forgetting the ½ gives 0.9 m.

q: Two bodies of equal mass, one moving due east at 3 m s⁻¹ and the other due north at 4 m s⁻¹, collide and stick together. Their common speed just after the collision is:
x: Total momentum = √((3m)² + (4m)²) = 5m, shared by mass 2m, so the speed is 5m/2m = 2.5 m s⁻¹. Averaging the two speeds as if they were in the same direction gives 3.5 m s⁻¹.

q: Ball X moving at 5 m s⁻¹ makes a head-on elastic collision with ball Y at rest. After the collision X continues forward at 1 m s⁻¹. The velocity of Y just after the collision is:
x: In an elastic head-on collision the speed of separation equals the speed of approach: v_Y − 1 = 5 − 0, so v_Y = 6 m s⁻¹. (Momentum then fixes m_X/m_Y = 1.5, consistent with the elastic formula.) Treating the masses as equal and using 5 − 1 gives 4 m s⁻¹.

q: Trolleys of mass 1 kg and 3 kg are held together at rest with a compressed spring between them, then released on a smooth floor. The ratio of their kinetic energies (1 kg trolley : 3 kg trolley) just after separation is:
x: Total momentum stays zero, so both trolleys have equal momentum p. K = p²/2m, so K ∝ 1/m and the ratio is 3 : 1. Check with speeds: 1 kg at 3v, 3 kg at v: ½(1)(9v²) : ½(3)(v²) = 9 : 3 = 3 : 1. 9 : 1 is the ratio of the squared speeds alone.

q: A 4 kg body moving at 5 m s⁻¹ collides head-on with a 1 kg body at rest. After the collision the 4 kg body moves on in the same direction at 3 m s⁻¹. The velocity of the 1 kg body and the type of collision are:
o: 8 m s⁻¹, and the collision is inelastic
8 m s⁻¹, and the collision is elastic
2 m s⁻¹, and the collision is elastic
2 m s⁻¹, and the collision is inelastic
x: Momentum: 4 × 5 = 4 × 3 + 1 × v, so v = 8 m s⁻¹. Kinetic energy before = ½(4)(25) = 50 J; after = ½(4)(9) + ½(1)(64) = 18 + 32 = 50 J, so it is elastic. Subtracting the speeds 5 − 3 gives the tempting 2 m s⁻¹.

q: Ignoring air resistance, the horizontal component of a projectile's velocity during its flight:
o: Decreases to zero at the highest point
Changes direction at the highest point
x: No horizontal force acts, so the horizontal velocity component stays constant. It is the vertical component that falls to zero at the highest point and then reverses.

q: Ignoring air resistance, a ball thrown from level ground with a fixed speed travels the greatest horizontal distance when it is thrown at an angle above the horizontal of:
x: Range R = v² sin 2θ/g is greatest when sin 2θ = 1, that is θ = 45°. At 90° the range is zero; 30° and 60° give equal but smaller ranges.

q: Two stones are projected from level ground with the same speed, one at 30° and the other at 60° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, they have equal:
x: R = v² sin 2θ/g, and sin 60° = sin 120°, so complementary angles give the same range. The 60° stone goes higher and stays up longer; the 30° stone has the larger horizontal velocity.

q: A ball is projected at 20 m s⁻¹ at 60° above the horizontal (cos 60° = 0.5). Ignoring air resistance, its speed at the highest point of its path is:
x: At the top the vertical component is zero, leaving only the constant horizontal component: 20 cos 60° = 10 m s⁻¹. Saying zero confuses this with a ball thrown straight up; 10√3 m s⁻¹ uses sin 60°.

q: A projectile launched from level ground at angle θ with speed v has range R. Ignoring air resistance, if it is launched at the same angle with speed 2v, its range becomes:
x: R = v² sin 2θ/g, so R ∝ v²: doubling the speed makes the range 4R. Taking R proportional to v gives 2R.

q: A projectile is launched from level ground so that its horizontal range is four times its maximum height. Ignoring air resistance, its angle of projection above the horizontal is:
x: R = 2v² sin θ cos θ/g and H = v² sin²θ/2g, so R/H = 4 cos θ/sin θ = 4/tan θ. R = 4H gives tan θ = 1, θ = 45°. Check at 45°: R = v²/g and H = v²/4g, ratio 4.

q: A ball is projected from level ground at 50 m s⁻¹ at 37° above the horizontal (sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8). Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², the horizontal distance it has covered when it reaches its highest point is:
x: Vertical: 50 × 0.6 = 30 m s⁻¹, so it reaches the top after 30/10 = 3 s; horizontal: 50 × 0.8 = 40 m s⁻¹, so it has gone 40 × 3 = 120 m. Check: full range = 2 × 50² × 0.6 × 0.8/10 = 240 m, and the top is halfway. 240 m is the whole range; 45 m is the maximum height.

q: Ignoring air resistance, at the highest point of a projectile's path the angle between its velocity and its acceleration is:
x: At the highest point the velocity is purely horizontal and the acceleration is g vertically downward, so they are at 90°. At launch the angle is greater than 90°; it is never 0° for a projectile launched at an angle.
